issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder based solely on circumstantial evidence requires every incriminating circumstance to be proved and the complete chain to exclude every reasonable hypothesis other than guilt.

In a case based on circumstantial evidence, proof of motive may provide an important corroborative link, but unsubstantiated family disputes and an unproved complaint do not establish motive for murder.

The prosecution must establish the foundational facts, including the accused’s presence with the deceased at the relevant time, before the burden to explain under Section 106 of the Evidence Act can shift to the accused.

An accused’s failure to explain facts within their special knowledge cannot support conviction under Section 106 of the Evidence Act where the prosecution has not established a complete chain of circumstances.
Failure to examine material witnesses without explanation and failure to produce relevant contemporaneous records may justify an adverse inference against the prosecution.
The benefit of an acquittal may be extended under Article 142 of the Constitution to a non-appealing co-accused whose case is identical to that of the appellants.
